title: What is stress? Acute and chronic
citation: Candeias, A. A., Galindo, E., Reschke, K., Bidzan, M., & Stueck, M. (2024). The interplay of stress, health, and well-being: unraveling the psychological and physiological processes. Frontiers in Psychology, 15, 1471084.
content:
What is stress? acute and chronic.

Stress is the body's natural response to demands, challenges, or change. It helps you react quickly when facing deadlines, solving problems, or dealing with unexpected situations. This short-term response is called acute stress, and it usually settles once the situation has passed. Chronic stress happens when the pressures continue for weeks or months without enough opportunity to recover. Over time, staying in this heightened state can begin to affect both physical and emotional wellbeing.

Isn't stress just a mindset problem?

People often hear that stress is just a mindset problem and that they simply need to think more positively. While our thoughts can influence how stressful something feels, stress is much more than a mindset. It is a whole body response involving the brain, nervous system, hormones, and immune system. Because stress affects the body as well as the mind, reducing stress is not simply about trying harder to stay calm.

Stress vs anxiety: what's the difference.

Stress and anxiety often feel similar because they activate many of the same physical responses, but they are not exactly the same. Stress usually develops in response to an identifiable pressure, such as work demands, financial concerns, or family responsibilities, and it often improves once the pressure reduces. Anxiety can continue even when there is no immediate stressor, as the brain remains focused on anticipating future threats. It is also common for prolonged stress to increase feelings of anxiety over time.

Why do I feel stressed when nothing's changed?

Sometimes people feel increasingly stressed even though nothing obvious has changed in their lives. Stress can build gradually as small demands accumulate without enough time to recover. Poor sleep, ongoing responsibilities, relationship difficulties, physical health problems, and long periods without rest can all increase the body's stress load. Because this build-up is often gradual, people may not realise how much pressure they have been carrying until they begin to feel overwhelmed.

When does stress become a problem I need help with?

Stress is a normal part of life, but it is worth seeking support if it becomes persistent, feels difficult to manage, or starts affecting your sleep, physical health, work, relationships, or ability to enjoy everyday life. Effective support may include evidence-based psychological therapies, stress management strategies, lifestyle changes, and addressing the sources of ongoing pressure where possible. Many people find that understanding how stress works is the first step towards regaining a sense of balance and wellbeing.
